grammar.title: Present perfect: have/has + past participle
grammar.explanation:
We use the **present perfect** to talk about past actions that are connected to the present. Form it with **have** or **has** + the **past participle** of the main verb: *I have visited*, *she has eaten*.

Use **have** with *I, you, we, they* and **has** with *he, she, it*: *they have arrived*, *he has arrived*.

We often use it for **life experiences** with *ever* and *never*: *Have you ever been to Japan? I have never tried sushi.* The exact time is not important — what matters is the experience itself.

We also use it for **recent actions** with *just*, *already*, and *yet*: *She has just finished. We have already seen it. Have you booked the hotel yet?*

For actions that started in the past and **continue now**, use it with **since** and **for**: *They have lived here since 2019. I have known him for ten years.*

Remember: the present perfect connects the past to **now**. If you say exactly when something happened (*yesterday*, *last week*), use the **past simple** instead: *I visited Rome last year.*
examples: I have visited three countries this year. (life experience, time not important)
She has just arrived at the terminal. (recent action with just)
Have you ever taken a ferry? (asking about experience with ever)
They have lived in this city since 2015. (started in the past, still true with since)
We have already reserved our hostel room. (already = sooner than expected)
He has never been on a cruise. (never = zero experience)
